newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour unveils plan for citizen's service.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour unveils plan for citizen's service.

text.p: A national force of 100,000 young "millennium volunteers" would be helping the elderly and disabled and cleaning up the community by the year 2000 under plans for a citizen's service unveiled on Wednesday by the Labour party.

Education and employment spokesman David Blunkett said the programme, to be designed in partnership with the voluntary sector and business, would give young people a chance to improve their skills and develop a new sense of responsibility.
"The chance to be rewarded and to be valued -- the chance to be part of our society, to identify and be welcomed, rather than rejected," Blunkett told the party's annual conference.

The service, which will cost 30 million stg to set up, is a key part of Labour's strategy for meeting its commitment to get 250,000 young people aged 18-25 off welfare by investing the proceeds of a windfall tax on privatised utilities.
Labour sees education as one of its strong suits in the forthcoming election. Blunkett said its lead in polls on the issue had widened to 36 percent from nine percent in 1992.
He also made the following pledges:
-- to offer a nursery place to all four-year-olds and to set targets to provide places for three-year-olds whose parents wish it. The current nursery voucher scheme will be abolished.
-- to establish centres of early excellence throughout Britain, starting with 25 pilot centres.
-- to make a start through a public/private partnership on the 3.2 billion stg backlog identified in the repair and maintenance of school buildings.
-- to phase out the assisted places scheme to pay for a reduction in class sizes so no five-seven year-olds are in a class of more than 30.
-- new three-week literacy summer schools to bring every youngster's reading skills up to scratch over the next decade.
